10.text: The inhabitants of the Eskimo village Nɵˊɵkan, on East Cape, who differ

11.text: in language from those on Indian Point, are called simply Nɵˊɵkalɪt, or, with

12.text: derision, Peˊekit.² The inhabitants of Wuteˊen, the last Eskimo village on

13.text: Cape Ulakhpen, to the northwest of Plover Bay, also differing in language

14.text: from those on Indian Point, are called in a similar way Wuteˊelɪt. Mr. Gondatti

15.text: maintains the opinion that the Nɵˊɵkalɪt and the Wuteˊelɪt cannot understand

16.text: the language spoken on Indian Point, and have to use Chukchee in speaking

17.text: with its inhabitants.³ Following in his footsteps, Mr. Bogdanovitch speaks of

18.text: the extensive mixing of peoples on the coast of the Chukchee Peninsula.⁴

19.text: However, from comparative texts in all three dialects, which I brought with

20.text: me, it is evident that the dialectic differences are not so great as Mr. Gondatti

21.text: supposes. Indeed, I had occasion several times to witness the people of all

22.text: three tribes conversing without difficulty, every one using his own dialect. Of

23.text: course, being conversant with the Chukchee language, they can also use it

24.text: for the same purpose. In any case, it is not necessary to assume for these
